14840:
Solemn describes something — or someone — that is deeply serious, dignified, and full of weight. It signals that a moment, a person's expression, a promise, or an atmosphere carries great importance and deserves full respect and quiet attention.

Think of it this way: when something is solemn, it feels too significant and meaningful to treat lightly or casually. There is a gravity to it — like an invisible force pressing down, saying "this matters deeply."

The word works in two closely related ways:

1. Describing an atmosphere, occasion, or setting

Some moments in life feel heavy with meaning — they are not the time for jokes, laughter, or casual chatter. A funeral is solemn. A war memorial is solemn. The moment a judge delivers a verdict in court is solemn. A candlelight vigil is solemn.

These are situations where people naturally slow down, lower their voices, and carry themselves with care and respect. The mood in the air is serious and dignified. That mood is solemn.

2. Describing a promise, oath, or commitment

When a person makes a solemn promise, they are not making a casual, throwaway statement. They mean it with their whole heart. It is sincere, binding, and deeply felt. A soldier takes a solemn oath to protect their country. A doctor takes a solemn oath to do no harm. These are not words spoken lightly — they carry a sense of sacredness and personal honor.

When you encounter something solemn, you feel a particular kind of quiet seriousness wash over you. It is not the same as feeling bored, or frightened, or angry. It is more like a calm, respectful stillness — an awareness that something important is unfolding.

Imagine walking into a grand, empty cathedral. No one is speaking. Light filters through stained glass. You naturally feel the urge to walk softly and speak in whispers. That feeling is the feeling of solemnity — and the cathedral, in that moment, feels solemn.

Or imagine the moment before a soldier is buried with military honors, and the flag is being folded in complete silence. Everyone stands still. No one laughs. The air itself seems to hold its breath. That is a solemn moment.

This is important, because learners often confuse "solemn" with similar words.

Solemn ≠ Sad. A solemn moment can feel sad, but sadness is not the definition. A graduation ceremony can be solemn — it is formal, dignified, and deeply meaningful — but it is also joyful. A wedding can have solemn moments (the exchange of vows) and happy moments (the celebration after). Solemnity is about seriousness and weight, not specifically about grief or sorrow.

Solemn ≠ Quiet. Something can be quiet without being solemn (a sleeping baby's room), and something can be solemn without being completely quiet (a solemn speech delivered before a crowd). The quiet associated with solemn moments comes from the respect people feel, not from the word itself.

Solemn ≠ Strict or Harsh. A strict teacher is demanding. A solemn teacher, in a given moment, is deeply serious and earnest — perhaps addressing something very important with the class. Strictness is about rules and discipline; solemnity is about depth of feeling and seriousness of purpose.

Solemn ≠ Boring or Dull. Something boring has no energy and fails to engage you. Something solemn has a different kind of energy — one that is quiet and weighty, but very much alive with meaning and significance.

Here are examples showing the word in action, covering its different uses:

  • The soldiers stood in solemn silence as the flag was lowered.

(The atmosphere was serious, respectful, and dignified.)

  • She made a solemn promise that she would never tell anyone the secret.

(The promise was deeply sincere and heartfelt — not casual.)

  • His face wore a solemn expression as he delivered the bad news.

(His face was serious and grave, showing the weight of the moment.)

  • The courtroom was quiet and solemn as the judge prepared to speak.

(The setting carried a formal, serious, respectful atmosphere.)

  • It was a solemn occasion — the entire country paused to remember those who had died.

(The event was formal, dignified, and charged with deep meaning.)

  • The children, usually loud and playful, became solemn when they visited the old war cemetery.

(They became serious and respectful in response to the weighty surroundings.)
How Solemn Feels on a Spectrum

It helps to see where "solemn" sits among related words:

Lighthearted → Serious → Grave → Solemn → Mournful

"Solemn" sits in the serious-to-grave zone. It is heavier than simply "serious" because it carries an element of formality, ceremony, or deep sincerity. But it is not as overwhelmed by grief as "mournful." It is seriousness with dignity.

Since you want full mastery:

  • Solemnly (adverb) — He solemnly swore to tell the truth. (He swore in a deeply serious and sincere way.)
  • Solemnity (noun) — The solemnity of the occasion moved everyone to tears. (The quality or state of being solemn — the seriousness, weight, and dignity of the moment.)
  • Solemnize (verb) — To solemnize a marriage means to perform it formally and with proper ceremony.

If you had to remember just one thing: solemn means deeply serious, dignified, and full of weight — whether describing a moment, a ceremony, a facial expression, or a promise — in a way that demands quiet respect and cannot be treated lightly.
14841:
Solemnity is the quality of being deeply serious, grave, and dignified — especially in a way that feels weighty, ceremonial, or sacred. It is the feeling that something truly matters, and that everyone present understands and respects that.

Think of it this way: not all seriousness is solemnity. If your boss is annoyed at a meeting, that is serious — but it is not solemn. Solemnity carries a special kind of gravity. It is calm, not tense. It is reverent, not harsh. It feels almost ceremonial by nature.

The word is used in two closely related ways:

1. As a quality or atmosphere
This is when you describe the feeling or mood of a moment, place, or person's manner. It answers the question: "What is the tone here?"

  • The courtroom was filled with solemnity as the verdict was read.
  • He spoke with great solemnity, and no one dared interrupt.
  • There was a quiet solemnity to the mountain at dawn.

Here, solemnity is like an invisible weight in the air — it signals to everyone that what is happening is serious and important.

2. As a formal ceremony or ritual
In this sense (especially in the plural, solemnities), the word refers to a formal, ceremonial act or observance itself — usually one tied to religion, law, or tradition.

  • The solemnities of the coronation lasted three hours.
  • The marriage was performed with all due solemnity and legal formality.
  • The church observed the solemnity of Good Friday with fasting and prayer.

Here, solemnity is the ceremony — the structured, formal event through which something important is officially and reverently marked.

To really understand the word, it helps to know what ingredients create solemnity. A moment or event tends to carry solemnity when it involves:

  • Gravity — it concerns something of real consequence: life, death, justice, sacred duty, national identity.
  • Dignity — it is handled with care, respect, and formality, never carelessly or cheaply.
  • Reverence — there is an unspoken acknowledgment that this moment deserves full attention and respect.
  • Stillness — not necessarily silence, but a deliberate, unhurried quality. No frivolity. No distraction.

When all of these come together, you have solemnity.

This is important, because learners often confuse solemnity with nearby ideas:

  • Solemnity is not sadness. A funeral has solemnity, yes — but so does a swearing-in ceremony for a president, a graduation, or a religious festival. These can be joyful and still solemn. The solemnity comes from the weight of the occasion, not from grief.
  • Solemnity is not silence. A solemn moment can involve music, spoken words, or a crowd. What matters is the tone, not the volume.
  • Solemnity is not stiffness or coldness. A solemn person is not being rude or unfriendly. They are being appropriately serious for the moment. There is warmth inside solemnity — especially in religious or communal settings.
  • Solemnity is not everyday seriousness. A doctor discussing a diagnosis is serious. A judge pronouncing a sentence is solemn. The difference is in the ceremony, weight, and reverence involved.

Solemnity exists on a spectrum. You can have:

  • A quiet solemnity — like a moment of silence at a war memorial.
  • A grand solemnity — like a papal mass in a cathedral before thousands.
  • A personal solemnity — when someone makes a promise with sincerity and gravity, even in private.
  • A legal solemnity — the formal acts required to make a contract, oath, or marriage legally valid.

The scale changes. The essence does not.

• "with great solemnity" — performed or spoken in a very formal, serious, dignified way.
  • "the solemnity of the occasion" — the serious, weighty nature of the event at hand.
  • "religious solemnity" — a sacred feast or ceremony in a church tradition.
  • "due solemnity" — the proper level of formality and seriousness that a situation requires.
  • "a sense of solemnity" — a feeling that a moment carries special weight and importance.
A Mental Image to Anchor It

Imagine a military general being buried with full honors. The flag is folded with precise, careful movements. Every officer stands perfectly still. Music plays slowly. No one speaks above a whisper. Every action says: "This person's life, and this moment, matter profoundly."

That atmosphere — that careful, reverent, dignified weight — is solemnity.

Now imagine that same feeling applied to a coronation, a wedding vow, a courtroom verdict, a religious mass, or even a great piece of music performed in perfect silence before an audience. Each of these can carry solemnity, because each involves gravity, dignity, and a shared understanding that something truly important is taking place.

That is the word in its full meaning.
14842:
Solemnly means doing or saying something with deep seriousness, genuine sincerity, and a strong sense that the moment truly matters — in a way that feels weighty, dignified, and fully intentional.

When someone does something solemnly, they are not being casual, playful, or careless. They are completely present in the moment, fully aware of its importance, and acting with their whole heart behind it.

Think of solemnly as carrying three things at once:

1. Seriousness — The person is not joking or being light about it. The tone is grave and controlled.

2. Sincerity — It is deeply, genuinely meant. There is no performance or pretending. What is being said or done comes from a place of true feeling or true commitment.

3. Weight / Gravity — There is a sense that this moment matters — that it has significance, consequence, or importance beyond the ordinary.

All three of these ingredients must be present. Something done solemnly is not just quiet, not just formal, and not just sad. It is all of these wrapped together: heavy with meaning, genuine, and treated with full respect.

The word can be used across a wide range of situations, and the meaning shifts slightly depending on context — but the core always stays the same.

In oaths and promises:
This is the most classic use. When someone solemnly swears or solemnly promises, they are making a commitment with their full sincerity behind it — not a casual "sure, I'll try." It means: I mean this completely, and I take full responsibility for it.

"I solemnly swear to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth."

You have heard this in courtroom dramas. The word solemnly here tells you this is not a casual statement — it is a binding, serious, morally-loaded commitment. The person is placing their integrity on the line.

In ceremonies and rituals:
Funerals, national ceremonies, religious events — these are places where things happen solemnly. The pace is slow, the tone is reverent, and everyone understands that this is not a moment for laughter or distraction.

"The soldiers solemnly lowered the flag as the sun set."

The soldiers move carefully, quietly, with full awareness of what the flag represents. There is dignity in their movement. That is what solemnly adds here.

In serious speech or announcements:
When someone speaks solemnly, their voice carries weight. They are not chatting — they are delivering something that must be received with full attention.

"The doctor solemnly told the family that there was no more they could do."

The doctor is not being cold or robotic. He is being entirely real, entirely careful with his words, entirely aware of the gravity of what he is saying.

In personal reflection or grief:
When someone stands solemnly at a grave or looks solemnly at a photo of someone they lost, they are in a state of quiet, deep feeling — respectful, still, and inward.

"She stood solemnly at her mother's grave, saying nothing."

No words are needed here. The stillness itself carries the solemnity.

It does not simply mean "sadly."
You can be sad and not solemn (like crying while watching a romantic movie). You can be solemn and not sad (like a dignified graduation ceremony). They can overlap, but sadness is not the definition.

It does not simply mean "quietly."
You can whisper and be casual. You can speak loudly and be solemn. The volume has nothing to do with it — it is the inner attitude that matters.

It does not mean "slowly."
Though solemn moments often do move at a slower pace, the speed itself is not the meaning. A solemn speech given quickly is still solemn if it carries that weight and sincerity.

It does not mean "formally" in a purely cold or bureaucratic way.
An office email sent in professional language is not solemn. Solemnity requires genuine feeling or genuine moral weight — a human sense of importance, not just a dress code.

Here is a helpful way to feel the word intuitively:

Imagine two people making the same promise — "I will always be there for you."

The first person says it lightly, in passing, almost automatically.

The second person stops, looks you in the eyes, and says the same words — slowly, with full intention, as if placing something precious in your hands.

The second person said it solemnly.

That pause, that directness, that weight — that is what solemnly captures. It signals to everyone around: this matters, and I know it matters, and I am treating it with the full respect it deserves.

Solemnly = seriously + sincerely + with deep awareness of the weight of the moment.

Use it when:

  • A promise, oath, or vow is made with full commitment
  • A ceremony is conducted with dignity and reverence
  • Something is said or done with heavy, genuine, undistracted seriousness
  • A moment of grief, remembrance, or duty is approached with full respect

The word always signals that the ordinary rules are suspended — no lightness, no carelessness, no half-measures. Only gravity, sincerity, and presence.
14843:
To solicit means to actively go out and ask someone for something — whether that's help, money, an opinion, a vote, business, or anything else you want or need.

The key word here is actively. When you solicit something, you are not sitting and waiting for it to come to you. You are making a deliberate, purposeful effort to seek it out, often approaching the other person first.

Think of soliciting as a kind of earnest, intentional asking. It usually carries a slightly formal or serious tone — more purposeful than a casual "hey, can you help me?" but not as desperate as begging.

There is also often a sense that you are asking someone who has the power to give you what you want — a donor who has money, a customer who has business to offer, a committee that makes decisions, or an authority that can grant a request.
The Different Ways It Is Used

1. Asking for money, help, or support

This is one of the most common uses. Organizations, charities, and campaigns solicit funds, volunteers, or support from people.

The charity went door to door, soliciting donations from residents.
The politician solicited support from voters in every neighborhood.

Here, solicit simply means they went out and actively sought those things.

2. Asking for opinions, feedback, or ideas

When a person or organization wants input, they solicit opinions or feedback. This is very common in professional and academic settings.

The manager solicited feedback from every employee before making the final decision.
The professor solicited questions from the class after the lecture.
The government solicited public opinion on the new policy before passing it.

In this use, it means they are formally and deliberately inviting people to share their thoughts.

3. Seeking business or customers

Companies, salespeople, or freelancers often solicit business or clients — meaning they actively approach potential customers to offer their services.

The salesperson called dozens of companies, soliciting new business.
The law firm solicited clients by sending letters to people involved in car accidents.

This is why you will sometimes see signs that say "No soliciting" on the doors of homes or offices — it means do not come here to sell things or ask for anything.

4. Formally requesting something in an official or professional context

In formal or institutional settings, organizations solicit bids, proposals, or applications — meaning they formally invite people or companies to submit offers.

The city council solicited bids from construction companies to build the new bridge.
The foundation solicited proposals from researchers looking for grant funding.

Here, solicit has a very official tone — it is a formal, public call for people to come forward with something.

5. Approaching someone to commit a crime (a serious use)

In legal language, to solicit can mean to urge, persuade, or pressure someone to do something illegal or wrong. This is a criminal act in most legal systems.

He was arrested for soliciting someone to commit fraud.

This is called criminal solicitation — you don't even have to commit the crime yourself; the act of asking or encouraging someone else to do it can be a crime on its own.

6. Approaching someone for sex in exchange for money

Soliciting is also a legal and common term for approaching someone, especially in a public place, to offer or seek paid sexual activity. This is illegal in most places and is treated as a criminal offense called solicitation.

She was charged with soliciting on a public street.

This use is specifically tied to law and criminal terminology, so you will see it mostly in legal or news contexts.

• Ask is plain and casual. "Can you help me?" — no special effort or formality implied.
  • Request is polite and slightly formal. It implies making a specific demand or wish known.
  • Beg implies desperation and a power imbalance — you are almost pleading.
  • Solicit implies active, deliberate effort to seek something out, often approaching people directly or formally, and often from multiple sources. It feels more purposeful and organized than the others.

Think of it this way: a child asks for a cookie. A customer requests a refund. A charity solicits donations by going out and approaching hundreds of people for them.
Unsolicited — A Word You Must Know

The opposite form, unsolicited, is extremely common and useful. It means something was given or done without being asked for.

He gave me unsolicited advice about how to raise my children — I never asked for his opinion.
I received an unsolicited email from a company trying to sell me something.

If something is solicited, you asked for it. If it's unsolicited, nobody asked — it arrived on its own, often unwelcomed.

• Solicitation (noun): The act of soliciting. "The email was a solicitation for donations."
  • Solicitor (noun): A person who solicits. Also, in the UK and some other countries, a solicitor is a type of lawyer who handles legal matters and advises clients (similar to an attorney in the US).
  • Unsolicited (adjective): Not asked for. "Unsolicited opinions are rarely welcome."
A Quick Summary to Lock It In

To solicit = to actively and purposefully go out and seek something from someone — money, opinions, business, votes, bids, or anything else.

It is formal, deliberate, and intentional. The person soliciting makes the first move. Depending on the context, it can be completely professional and neutral (soliciting feedback), commercially driven (soliciting business), or illegal and criminal (soliciting a crime, soliciting for sex).

When in doubt, just remember: you go out and seek it — that's soliciting.
14844: The word "solicitor" has three distinct meanings depending on where it is used. Each meaning is important and common in its own context.
Meaning 1: A Type of Lawyer (UK, Australia, and Commonwealth Countries)

In countries that follow the British legal tradition — such as the United Kingdom, Australia, Canada, and historically India — the legal profession is divided into two separate types of lawyers: solicitors and barristers.

A solicitor is the lawyer you go to first. When you have a legal problem, you hire a solicitor. They are the front-facing lawyers — the ones who deal with clients directly, give advice, and handle the paperwork.

What a solicitor does:

  • Listens to your legal problem and gives you advice
  • Drafts legal documents: wills, contracts, agreements, deeds
  • Helps you buy or sell property (this is called conveyancing)
  • Handles divorces, custody battles, and family matters
  • Sets up businesses and writes partnership agreements
  • Represents you in lower courts (like magistrates' courts or county courts)
  • If your case needs to go to a higher court (like the High Court), the solicitor hires a barrister to argue the case on your behalf

Think of it this way: a solicitor is your personal legal advisor and document handler. They prepare everything and manage your case. A barrister is a specialist court advocate hired by the solicitor (not directly by you) to argue in serious or complex court hearings. In everyday legal life, most people only ever deal with solicitors — not barristers.

In the UK, solicitors must register with the Solicitors Regulation Authority (SRA), which oversees their professional conduct.

Solicitor-advocates: In recent years, experienced solicitors can qualify as "solicitor-advocates," allowing them to also argue cases in higher courts — a right traditionally reserved for barristers. This blurs the line between the two roles slightly, but the fundamental distinction still stands.

Example sentences:

  • "I'm meeting with my solicitor tomorrow to finalise my will."
  • "She hired a solicitor to handle the purchase of her new house."
  • "The company's solicitor reviewed the contract before anyone signed it."

In the United States, "solicitor" does not refer to a private lawyer (Americans use "attorney" or "lawyer" for that). Instead, in the US, a solicitor is a government-employed legal official — a lawyer who works for a city, state, or federal government body.

Key examples:

  • City Solicitor (or Town Solicitor): The chief lawyer for a city or town government. This person advises the mayor and city council, reviews city contracts, represents the city in lawsuits, and handles all legal matters on the city's behalf. They are, essentially, the city's in-house lawyer.
  • Solicitor General: A very high-ranking official in the U.S. federal government, sitting within the Department of Justice. The Solicitor General represents the United States government in cases before the Supreme Court of the United States — deciding which cases the government will argue, appeal, or drop. It is one of the most prestigious legal positions in the country.
  • Solicitor of Labor / Solicitor of the Interior: Some federal departments (like the Department of Labor or the Department of the Interior) have their own senior legal officers with the title of "Solicitor," who manage all legal work within that department.

Example sentences:

  • "The city solicitor advised the council that the new ordinance was legally sound."
  • "The Solicitor General argued the government's case before the Supreme Court."
Meaning 3: Someone Who Asks for Business or Donations (Everyday American English)

Outside of the legal world, especially in everyday American English, a "solicitor" is simply a person who approaches others to ask for something — usually money, business, or support. This could happen door to door, over the phone, via email, or in person in a public place.

Common examples:

  • A charity worker going door to door collecting donations is a solicitor.
  • A salesperson calling you at home trying to sell you a product is a solicitor.
  • A political campaign worker knocking on doors asking for votes or donations is a solicitor.

You will very commonly see signs outside homes, offices, and apartment buildings that say "No Solicitors" or "No Soliciting." This means: "Do not come here to sell things, ask for money, or promote services. You are not welcome." It is a polite but firm notice to door-to-door sellers and charity workers.

Example sentences:

  • "A solicitor from the charity knocked on my door asking for a monthly donation."
  • "The office building had a 'No Solicitors' sign at the entrance."
Meaning 4: Legal Solicitation (In Criminal Law, Mostly US)

In criminal law, especially in the United States, the verb "to solicit" and the noun form carry a more serious meaning. Solicitation is a crime in which someone asks, encourages, or hires another person to commit an illegal act.

For example:

  • Soliciting prostitution = approaching someone and offering or asking for sex in exchange for money (illegal in most places)
  • Soliciting a bribe = asking someone to pay you illegally to do something in your position of authority
  • Solicitation of murder = trying to hire someone to kill another person

In these legal contexts, a "solicitor" would be the person doing the soliciting — the one making the unlawful request or offer.

Example sentences:

  • "He was arrested on charges of soliciting an undercover officer."
  • "The official was accused of soliciting bribes from contractors."
A Quick Summary of All Meanings

Where / Context → What it means:

  • UK / Australia / Commonwealth countries → A private lawyer you hire directly for legal advice, documents, and representation in lower courts.
  • USA (official/government context) → A government lawyer, especially a city solicitor (the city's lawyer) or the Solicitor General (who argues before the Supreme Court).
  • USA (everyday context) → A person asking for money, donations, or business, often door to door or by phone.
  • Criminal law (USA & elsewhere) → A person who unlawfully asks or pays someone to commit an illegal act.

1. Context is everything. The same word means very different things depending on the country and situation. If you see "solicitor" in a British legal drama, it means a lawyer. If you see a "No Solicitors" sign in America, it means salespeople. Keep context in mind.
  2. In India: Historically, there were solicitors and advocates as separate categories of legal professionals. Today, the term "advocate" is used almost universally in India under the Advocates Act, 1961. The Solicitors Act, 1961 still technically exists, and the Incorporated Law Society in Bombay (Mumbai) still has enrolled solicitors, but it is a rare and declining designation.
  3. A solicitor is NOT a notary. A notary public (or notary) is a different official who witnesses and authenticates signatures on documents. While solicitors can also do such work, the roles are not the same.
  4. In the UK, a solicitor and a barrister are both lawyers, but they do different things. You hire a solicitor directly. A solicitor hires a barrister for you if needed. You cannot (in most cases) approach a barrister yourself directly.
  5. The plural is simply "solicitors." There is no irregular form.

That covers every major and minor meaning of "solicitor" in the contexts where you are likely to encounter it, with enough detail to fully understand and use the word correctly for the rest of your life.
14845:
Solicitous means showing a deep, active, attentive kind of concern for someone's well-being, comfort, or happiness — the kind of concern that makes you go out of your way to make sure the other person is okay.

The keyword here is active. A solicitous person doesn't just feel concern quietly on the inside. They express it outwardly through careful attention and considerate action.

Think of a nurse who keeps checking on a patient — adjusting the pillow, asking about pain levels, making sure the room isn't too cold. Or a host at a dinner party who keeps asking if you need anything, refills your glass before it's empty, and ensures you feel completely at ease. That is solicitous behavior. It's care in motion.

The word has two closely related meanings. The first is by far the more common one.

Meaning 1 — Showing attentive, caring concern for someone:
This is the everyday use. Someone is solicitous when they are watchfully, earnestly concerned about another person's comfort, health, or happiness.

"She was solicitous about her elderly father's health, calling him every evening and arranging his doctor's appointments herself."

"The hotel staff were remarkably solicitous, anticipating the guests' needs before they even had to ask."

Meaning 2 — Being eager or anxious to do or achieve something:
This is a more formal use, and it means being keenly desirous or nervously eager to accomplish something.

"He was solicitous to make a good impression on his first day at work."

"The young diplomat was solicitous to avoid any diplomatic offense."

Notice that in Meaning 2, the concern isn't directed at a person's comfort, but at getting something right. The underlying feeling is the same — a kind of anxious, focused desire — but the object is different.

What separates solicitous from plain, ordinary caring is the quality of anxious eagerness wrapped inside it. A solicitous person isn't relaxed about the other person's welfare. There's a slight tension in it — a quiet, underlying need to make sure everything is right.

This is important. The word captures both the warmth of caring and the slight restlessness of worry. It's not just "I care about you." It's closer to "I care about you, and I want to make sure you're alright, and I'll keep checking until I'm sure."

By itself, solicitous is a positive or neutral word. It describes a genuinely admirable quality — thoughtful, warm attentiveness toward others.

However, context can push it in a more critical direction. When you see phrases like "overly solicitous" or "too solicitous," the writer is suggesting that someone's attentiveness has crossed a line into fussiness, hovering, or smothering concern. Imagine a waiter who interrupts your dinner conversation every two minutes to ask if everything is alright. Or a parent who is so worried about their adult child that they call three times a day. That kind of excessive attentiveness can be described as too solicitous.

So the word itself is complimentary, but it lives near the edge of a behavior that can tip into being overbearing.
How It Differs from Similar Words

These words are all in the same neighborhood, but they are not the same.

Concerned is more neutral and internal. You can be concerned without doing anything about it. Solicitous implies that the concern has translated into outward, attentive action.

Caring describes a general quality of character. It's broad and warm, but it doesn't carry the specific sense of active, watchful attentiveness that solicitous does.

Attentive focuses on the act of paying close attention. Solicitous adds an emotional layer on top — the underlying worry and desire for the other person's well-being that motivates that attention.

Considerate is about being thoughtful of others' feelings. Solicitous is stronger — it suggests a more urgent, watchful concern, not just politeness.

Think of it this way: a considerate person holds the door open for you. A solicitous person holds the door open, asks if you need help carrying your bags, makes sure you've eaten, and checks later that you got home safely.

Solicitous is a formal, somewhat elevated word. You are far more likely to meet it in literary fiction, careful journalism, formal essays, or polished speech than in casual everyday conversation. It lends writing a tone of refinement and precision.

In casual speech, someone might simply say "he was so caring" or "she kept fussing over us." In more formal or literary writing, the same idea would be captured with "he was solicitous" or "she was solicitous of their comfort."

Here are the most natural ways the word is used in a sentence:

  • Solicitous about something → "She was solicitous about his recovery."
  • Solicitous of someone's comfort/needs → "He was solicitous of his guests' every need."
  • Solicitous to do something → "They were solicitous to avoid any offense."

Knowing the related forms will help you recognize this word in the wild:

Solicitously (adverb) — describes how something is done with care and concern.

"He solicitously arranged the blanket around her shoulders."

Solicitude (noun) — the state or feeling of being solicitous; deep, attentive concern.

"She was touched by the solicitude her colleagues showed during her illness."
One Final Image to Lock It In

If you want one image to anchor this word in your memory forever:

Picture a devoted grandmother who, the moment you walk through her door, immediately wants to know — are you cold? Are you hungry? Did you sleep enough? Let her get you something to eat. Here, sit in this comfortable chair. She is not asking out of habit or politeness. She is genuinely, actively, almost anxiously focused on making sure you are perfectly comfortable and well. That grandmother, in that moment, is the very picture of solicitous.
14846:
Solicitude is a deep, careful concern for someone's well-being, comfort, or safety — one that is warm and caring on the inside, but tinged with worry or anxiety on the outside.

Think of it this way: when you care about someone, you feel good things toward them. But when you feel solicitude, that care becomes so strong and so focused that it starts to feel a little like worry. You are not just fond of them — you are actively thinking about them, watching over them, hoping they are okay, and quietly anxious that they might not be.

Solicitude sits at the intersection of three feelings:

Love/Care + Worry + Attentiveness = Solicitude

It is never cold or detached. It always comes from a place of genuine warmth. But it is also not carefree or relaxed — there is always a slight undercurrent of concern running through it. A person feeling solicitude is not simply wishing someone well and moving on. They are dwelling on that person's condition. They are paying close, careful, almost watchful attention.
What Makes It Different from Similar Words

This is important, because "solicitude" is often confused with words that are close but not quite the same.

Care is broad and general. You can "care" about thousands of things casually. Solicitude is narrower, deeper, and more emotionally loaded.

Worry leans toward the anxious, fearful side, and can be selfish in nature (you worry because you feel uncomfortable). Solicitude, by contrast, is outward-facing — it is entirely about the other person and their welfare.

Concern is perhaps the closest word, but it is flatter and more neutral. Solicitude is warmer, more tender, and more personal than concern. Solicitude has a human touch that plain "concern" often lacks.

Empathy is about understanding another person's feelings. Solicitude goes further — it is not just understanding, but actively, almost restlessly, caring about what happens to them.

Solicitude can appear in a few different flavors depending on the context:

1. Tender solicitude — the gentle, loving watchfulness of a parent over a sick child, or a close friend checking in on someone going through a hard time. It is soft and quiet.

2. Anxious solicitude — when the concern becomes more intense and worried. A spouse waiting for a loved one to come home safe in a storm. A doctor anxiously monitoring a patient. The caring is real, but the anxiety is louder here.

3. Dutiful solicitude — concern shown as a matter of deep responsibility. A nurse attending to a patient with careful, dedicated attention. A leader who loses sleep over the welfare of those who depend on them.

4. Excessive solicitude — solicitude can also be used to describe concern that goes too far, to the point of smothering or hovering. In this shade, it carries a slight negative tone — implying that the person's concern, though well-meaning, is suffocating or unnecessary.

To make this concrete, here are sentences that show the word in action:

  • "She watched over her elderly mother with great solicitude, making sure she ate well and felt no pain."

(Here: tender, loving watchfulness.)

  • "His solicitude for his students' futures was evident in the hours he spent mentoring them after class."

(Here: deep, responsible concern that goes beyond the minimum.)

  • "The ambassador spoke with visible solicitude about the plight of the refugees, his voice low and serious."

(Here: genuine, heartfelt concern about others' suffering.)

  • "Her excessive solicitude over her teenage son was beginning to feel more like surveillance than love."

(Here: the negative shade — concern that has crossed a line.)

It is not pity. Pity looks down at someone. Solicitude stands beside them.

It is not obsession. Obsession is self-centered and possessive. Solicitude is genuinely about the other person's welfare.

It is not indifference dressed up as politeness. Solicitude is always sincere. You cannot truly feel solicitude without actually caring.

If you want to remember this word for life, anchor it to this image:

A person who cannot fully relax because they keep thinking about whether someone they love is alright.

That quiet, warm, watchful, slightly worried state of mind — that is solicitude.

Since this is the noun form, it helps to know the family:

Solicitous (adjective) — the describing word. "She was solicitous about his health." This means: showing or feeling solicitude.

Solicitously (adverb) — the manner of doing something. "He asked solicitously whether she had eaten."

Knowing these forms means you will recognize the word even when it appears in a different shape in your reading.

In one sentence: Solicitude is the warm, attentive, slightly anxious concern you feel for someone you genuinely care about — a deep wish for their well-being that keeps you watching over them, even when there is nothing more you can do.
14847:
Solidarity means a powerful sense of unity among a group of people — a feeling of "we are in this together" — along with the active support and loyalty that comes from that feeling.

When people are in solidarity with each other, they recognize that they share something important: a struggle, a cause, a condition, or a goal. And because of that shared bond, they stand up for one another, protect one another, and work together — even when it costs them something personally.

Think of it like this: if your entire class refuses to take an exam because one student was treated unfairly, the class is acting in solidarity. Nobody is personally harmed by the exam, but everyone stands together for the person who was wronged.

Solidarity has two sides to it — an inner side and an outer side.

The inner side is the feeling: a deep sense of connection, shared identity, and mutual loyalty. It's the feeling that what hurts you also hurts me, and what lifts you also lifts me — even if we are different people living different lives.

The outer side is the action: actually doing something to show that unity. Speaking up, sacrificing comfort, joining a protest, going on strike, donating, boycotting — any action taken specifically because you stand with others.

Both sides matter. Solidarity that stays only as a feeling but never becomes action is considered weak or even hollow. Real solidarity shows up in behavior.
Solidarity vs. Words That Sound Similar

This is where most learners get confused, so let's untangle it carefully.

Solidarity vs. Sympathy
Sympathy means you feel sorry for someone from a distance. You feel for them, but you remain separate. Solidarity means you stand with them. You don't just feel sorry — you actively take their side and commit yourself to their cause.

A wealthy person might sympathize with homeless people without being in solidarity with them. A housing rights activist who organizes campaigns, speaks out, and advocates for policy change is acting in solidarity — even if they've never been homeless themselves.

Solidarity vs. Charity
Charity flows from a position of "I have more, so I'll give some to you." It is generous, but it keeps a distance between the giver and the receiver. Solidarity is more equal — it's not about giving to someone, it's about standing beside them.

Solidarity vs. Agreement
You don't have to agree with every belief or decision a person makes in order to be in solidarity with them. You only need to recognize that their cause or struggle is just and deserving of support.

For example, you might disagree with some of a labor union's specific demands, but still stand in solidarity with workers fighting against dangerous working conditions.
Where You'll See the Word Used

1. Labor and worker movements
This is perhaps the most classic use. Workers who go on strike together, refuse to cross a picket line, or resist their employer as a united front are showing solidarity. The famous slogan "an injury to one is an injury to all" captures exactly what solidarity means in this context.

2. Social and political movements
Groups fighting for civil rights, gender equality, LGBTQ+ rights, or racial justice constantly use the language of solidarity. When one marginalized group publicly supports another, that is solidarity. When people who are not directly affected by an injustice still speak out and march, that is solidarity.

3. International relations
Countries or people across the world can express solidarity with those suffering under war, disaster, or oppression — by sending aid, applying political pressure, holding vigils, or loudly condemning the wrongdoing.

4. Community and personal life
Even in everyday life, solidarity exists. Neighbors who come together after a flood, friends who stand beside someone being bullied, or a community that rallies behind a grieving family — these are all acts of solidarity on a personal scale.

What makes solidarity more than just "teamwork" or "support" is its moral weight. Solidarity usually implies:

  • A recognition of shared humanity or shared struggle. You see yourself in others' pain or fight.
  • A willingness to sacrifice. True solidarity often requires giving something up — time, comfort, money, safety, or convenience — for the benefit of others.
  • Collective power. Solidarity is the understanding that people are stronger together than apart. It's the force that turns individuals into a movement.

This is why the word carries such emotional and political power. It's not a light word. When someone says "I stand in solidarity with you," they are making a serious declaration — not just of sympathy, but of loyalty and commitment.

• "The miners refused to return to work, standing in solidarity with their injured colleagues."
  • "People around the world lit candles in solidarity with the victims of the earthquake."
  • "Despite their differences, the two communities showed remarkable solidarity during the crisis."
  • "The statement called for solidarity among all nations to combat climate change."
  • "Her solidarity with the protesters meant she was willing to lose her job to speak out."

Solidarity is the deep, active unity among people who stand together — especially in times of struggle or injustice — supporting and protecting one another as if each person's wellbeing were everyone's shared responsibility.
14848:
To solidify something means to make it solid, firm, or stable — or for something to become solid, firm, or stable on its own.

That's the heart of the word. But it lives in two worlds: the physical world and the abstract world. Both are equally important and widely used.

In its literal, physical sense, solidify means to change from a liquid (or sometimes a gas) into a solid state. It refers to the process of something hardening or setting.

Examples:

  • Water solidifies into ice when the temperature drops below 0°C.
  • Leave the melted chocolate in the fridge, and it will solidify in an hour.
  • The volcano's lava solidified as it cooled, forming new rock.
  • The glue needs time to solidify before you can handle the broken piece.

Notice something important: solidify can work in two directions:

  • You can solidify something (you cause it to become solid): "The cold air solidified the wax." — Here, you are doing the action to something else. This is called transitive use.
  • Something can solidify on its own (it becomes solid by itself): "The wax solidified overnight." — Here, the thing itself undergoes the change. This is called intransitive use.

Both are correct and natural.

This is where the word becomes truly powerful and is perhaps used even more often in everyday life. In this sense, solidify means to make something stronger, more certain, more stable, or more permanent — or for something to become that way.

Think of it this way: just as a liquid becomes firm and stable when it solidifies, an idea, a relationship, a plan, or a position can also "solidify" — meaning it becomes firmer, more established, and harder to shake.

Examples:

  • Winning three tournaments in a row solidified her reputation as the best player in the country.

(Her reputation became firm and unquestionable.)

  • The two countries signed a treaty to solidify their alliance.

(The alliance was made stronger and more permanent.)

  • After months of uncertainty, our business plan finally solidified.

(The plan became clear, stable, and decided.)

  • That one conversation solidified my decision to quit the job.

(The decision became final and firm in my mind.)

  • Spending time together during the trip solidified their friendship.

(Their friendship grew stronger and more lasting.)
The Key Relationship Between the Two Meanings

The figurative meaning is directly inspired by the physical meaning. When something liquid becomes solid, it:

  • Stops flowing (it's no longer uncertain or changing)
  • Holds its shape (it becomes stable)
  • Becomes harder (it's difficult to break or undo)

All of these qualities are what we mean when we use solidify in the abstract sense. A plan that solidifies is no longer vague and shifting — it has taken a clear shape. A relationship that solidifies is no longer fragile — it has become strong and lasting. A reputation that solidifies is no longer questionable — it is firmly established.

In the figurative sense, here are the kinds of things that are commonly solidified:

  • A position or lead — "The team solidified their lead in the second half."
  • A reputation or status — "The award solidified her status as a legend."
  • A relationship or alliance — "The deal solidified the partnership between the two companies."
  • A plan or idea — "After our meeting, the concept began to solidify."
  • A decision — "Seeing the results solidified my decision."
  • Power or control — "The new law solidified the government's control over the industry."
  • Support or a base — "He worked hard to solidify his support among voters."
  • Gains or progress — "The team worked to solidify the gains they had made."

Here are all the forms you'll encounter:

FormExample
solidify (base)"These events will solidify trust."
solidifies (he/she/it)"Cold weather solidifies the oil."
solidified (past)"Their bond solidified over time."
solidifying (in progress)"The plan is solidifying."

When you use solidify in the abstract sense, it almost always carries a positive or at least neutral tone. It suggests that something uncertain, weak, or fluid has become stable and established — and that is generally seen as a good or desirable outcome.

However, context matters. "The dictator solidified his grip on power" uses the word accurately, but the situation itself is negative. The word is neutral — it simply describes the process of becoming firm or established, regardless of whether the outcome is good or bad.

Physical sense: harden, set, freeze, congeal, coagulate, crystallize

Figurative sense: strengthen, cement, reinforce, consolidate, establish, entrench, firm up, confirm

Among these, cement and consolidate are the closest synonyms in the figurative sense and are often interchangeable with solidify.

Physical sense: melt, liquefy, dissolve, soften, thaw

Figurative sense: weaken, undermine, erode, shake, loosen, destabilize

Solidify means to make something solid, firm, and stable — or to become that way. Literally, it's about matter changing state (liquid → solid). Figuratively, it's about something uncertain or fragile becoming strong, established, and lasting. It is almost always a sign that something previously shaky has found its firm footing.
14849:
To soliloquize means to speak your thoughts aloud to yourself — not to another person, but as a spoken expression of what is happening inside your own mind. It is essentially thinking out loud in full sentences, as if you were narrating your own inner world to no one in particular.

The key idea here is that the speaking is real, but the audience is absent (or ignored). You are not having a conversation. You are not expecting a reply. You are simply letting your inner thoughts pour out through your voice.

This word is most at home in the world of theatre and drama. When an actor on stage pauses the action of the play and speaks their character's private thoughts aloud — not to any other character, but as if they are alone with their mind — they are soliloquizing. The speech itself is called a soliloquy.

The most famous example in all of literature is from Shakespeare's Hamlet. When Hamlet stands alone and says "To be or not to be — that is the question," he is not talking to anyone on stage. He is wrestling, out loud, with the deepest questions of his life. That is a soliloquy. And the act of delivering it is soliloquizing.

Why is this technique used in theatre? Because the playwright needs to let the audience inside a character's head. Since a character cannot literally broadcast their thoughts, they speak them aloud instead. It is a dramatic device — a window into the soul.

You do not need a stage to soliloquize. In real life, to soliloquize simply means to talk to yourself in a sustained, reflective way — especially about something you are working through emotionally or mentally.

Imagine someone pacing the kitchen, saying things like: "Why did I say that? I should have just kept quiet. But then again, someone had to say it..." — that person is soliloquizing. They are not talking to the room. They are processing their own thoughts through spoken words.
What Makes It Different from Just "Talking to Yourself"

Talking to yourself can be as small as saying "Where did I put my keys?" aloud. That is casual and trivial.

Soliloquizing carries more weight. It implies something more sustained, more reflective, and often more emotionally charged. When you soliloquize, you are usually working through something real — a decision, a conflict, a regret, a feeling. It has the quality of a speech, even if the only listener is the air around you.
How It Differs from Similar Words

Monologue — A monologue is a long speech delivered by one person, but it is addressed to other people (an audience or other characters). A monologue is outward-facing. A soliloquy — and therefore soliloquizing — is inward-facing.

Musing — To muse is to think deeply, but it can happen entirely in silence. To soliloquize requires speaking aloud. The voice is essential.

Ruminating — Ruminating is turning something over and over in your mind, and it is usually internal. Soliloquizing is ruminating that has found a voice.

• To soliloquize — the verb. "He tends to soliloquize when he is anxious."
  • A soliloquy — the noun. The actual speech or instance of soliloquizing. "Her soliloquy lasted ten minutes."
  • A soliloquist — a rare noun for a person who soliloquizes.

• After everyone left the room, she began to soliloquize about whether she had made the right choice.
  • The old professor would often soliloquize at his desk, speaking his arguments aloud before writing them down.
  • In the third act, the villain soliloquizes, and for the first time, the audience understands his true motive.
  • He caught himself soliloquizing in the shower again — full sentences, complete arguments, addressed to no one.
To soliloquize is to give voice to your private thoughts — to speak them aloud, alone, as though your inner world has briefly stepped outside yourself and begun to talk.
